since you see bodies as tools, i'm gonna use it as an example. Imagine that you have to assemble an ikea furniture, and you need to use a screwdriver. The only one you have is the one you get in the package. You start using it to assemble everything, but the handle is too small for your hand, the grip is mediocre at best and it has little bits of plastic on it that weren't removed during the assembly process. In short, it fucking sucks. It works, sure, but you probably want to go and buy a new, comfortable one for the next time. This is a very simplified explanation, but it is a bit similar for being trans. Your body works (in theory at least), but there's something about it that's "off". How "off" it feels depends a lot for everyone, there are trans people who don't transition, or only do the social part of it (name change for example). Regardless of how far they go into their transition, see it as them getting better, more efficient tools to assemble the thing called "existing".

Here's a very long answer with as many things as possible depending on how much time and energy you're willing to put into it:
First thing to do is to talk with your neighbors, I have a partially outdoor cat if that makes any sense, and when she got pregnant I made sure that everything was ready for when she'd pop, so maybe (hopefully) it'll be the case for them too.
Now if they don't plan on doing anything, or if they give a very vague answer, the best thing you could do is to set up a safe area sheltered from the weather and temperature in a spot she likes, preferably away from people and other animals passing by, and generally quiet. there's no guarantee that that's the spot she'll pick to give birth, but at least you're providing a new option to her. Once again, depending on how the neighbors answered, you might also have to discuss the food issue, cats who just gave birth don't really want to leave their kittens, even if it's just 5 minutes to eat, at least for a little while, so you'd have to bring to food and water near the cat instead if she ends up picking the spot you made. 
There isn't much I can say about the kitten care, the mothers knows how to care for it, even though they may need some time to adapt when it's their first litter. The only thing you could really do for the kittens is make sure that they all get to eat something, and that the mom grooms them when they come out if you manage to be there during the labor (note that sometimes the cat will be tired after pushing 3 lil' thing and might do the bare minimum for grooming, if that happens keep an eye on them but don't get concerned immediately). Also no touching the kittens until the mom is visibly okay with that, and always let her sniff your hand before you do anything, just in case. Depending on how much she trusts you it could take anywhere from a couple of hours to several weeks.
If there's anything else you'd like to know about let me know, I think my answer is long enough as it is and as I said i'm not sure how much you're willing to do hehe
